newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH MINISTER SEES NO CHANGE TO NATO PLANS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH MINISTER SEES NO CHANGE TO NATO PLANS.

text.p: A summit meeting between the Russian and American leaders is unlikely to bring big changes in either side's views of NATO expansion, a senior Czech official said on Friday.

Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin are scheduled to meet in Helsinki on March 20-21 when the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's enlargement plans, vehemently opposed by Moscow, will be a key topic.

"Helsinki will not mean that Russia will approve the enlargement or that NATO will say 'we withdraw our decision'," Czech Deputy Foreign Minister Karel Kovanda told a news conference, speaking through an interpreter.

The Czech Republic is a leading candidate to be among the first new members of NATO. The alliance is expected to invite prospective new members for further negotiations after a summit in Madrid in July and Kovanda said he was confident the Czech Republic would be among them.

"Nobody at our ministry can imagine that the Madrid summit would issue invitations to some countries and that the Czech Republic would not get one," he said after a seminar on the future of NATO's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme.
Poland and Hungary are also seen as likely candidates.
Kovanda said that after the planned enlargement, NATO would have to enhance the PFP to allow more political and military cooperation between members.

"The discussion has shown that the PFP will have to be enlarged and enhanced to fulfill especially the concerns of partnership countries and the interests in having more close cooperation in the political and military sphere," he said.
Kovanda said the PFP, designed to forge closer links between NATO and former Warsaw Pact countries, would remain an importnat forum also for countries not joining the alliance.
"In the future for us, hopefully as a member country of the alliance, the mechanism will serve for intensive cooperation rfor countries who wish to cooperate but are not members of NATO," he said.
The Prague seminar was also attended by representatives of Russia, which has agreed to join the PFP.
Kovanda said the Russian officials had, among other concerns, reiterated Moscow's opposition to new members having nuclear weapons on their territory.
Clinton and Yeltsin will be discussing a possible future agreement between NATO and Russia. Moscow wants a commitment that NATO will not move its military infrastructure eastwards.
